##Problem 1

```{r load}
library(tidyverse)

library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")

glimpse(ny_noaa)
```
```{r data-summary}
#To view the number of weather stasions & date rage
station_summary = ny_noaa %>%
  summarise(
    n_stations = n_distinct(id),
    first_date = min(date, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_date = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

print(station_summary)

missing_summary = ny_noaa %>%
  summarise(
    #view the number of the missing value in every column
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))
  ) %>%
  #Change the data missing-value table form horizonal to vertical
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_n"
  ) %>%
  #Calculate the missing percentage for each variable
  mutate(
    missing_percent = 100 * missing_n / nrow(ny_noaa)
  )

missing_summary

```
The NY NOAA dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables from 747 weather stations in New York State, covering from January 1, 1981, through December 31, 2010. Each row represents a daily weather record for one station. The variables include station ID (`id`), observation date(`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).

There are no missing values in `id` or `date`. However, 5.62% of precipitation values, 14.69% of snowfall values, and 22.80% of snow depth values are missing. Both maximum and minimum temperature have about 43.71% missing values. Missing data are therefore a substantial issue, like for temperature analyses. And it could affect comparisons across stations and years if missingness varies between these groups.

```{r cleaning}
#Cleaning data
noaa_clean = ny_noaa %>%
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10,
    prcp = prcp/10
  )

glimpse(noaa_clean)
summary(
  select(noaa_clean, tmax, tmin, prcp, snow, snwd)
)

```
```{r snowfall}
snowfall_counts = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(snow)) %>%
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

snowfall_counts
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm. Because many days have no snowfall.


```{r monthly-temperature, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#Average maximum temperatures in January and July
monthly_temp = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(
    month %in% c(1, 7),
    !is.na(tmax)
  ) %>%
  group_by(id, year, month) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax),
    n_days = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

ggplot(
  monthly_temp,
  aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "blue", size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station and year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

July is much warmer than January, and January shows larger changes across years. Many stations follow similar patterns, with some years being warmer or colder than others. For example, January 2003 looks especially cold.

There are also a few possible outliers. One station has an unusually low July average of about 14°C around 1988.


```{r temperature-relationship, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
#Temperature relationship & snowfall distribution
temperature_plot = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(tmax),
    !is.na(tmin)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 70) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    transform = "log10",
    name = "Count"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum versus minimum temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

temperature_plot

```

```{r snowfall-distribution, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year
snowfall_plot = noaa_clean %>%
  filter(
    snow > 0,
    snow < 100
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "green",
    outlier.size = 0.5,
    outlier.alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall distribution by year",
    subtitle = "Daily snowfall greater than 0 and less than 100 mm",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)
  )

snowfall_plot
```


```{r combined-plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=10}
library(patchwork)

combined_plot = (temperature_plot / snowfall_plot) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

combined_plot
```
Maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive relationship with a few unusual observations away from the main pattern.

Snowfall distributions are fairly similar across years, with medians around 25 mm. Some years, such as 2006, have a smaller interquartile range. There is no clear long-term trend among daily snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 mm.


##Problem 2
```{r import-nhanes}
#Import data
covar_raw = read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
  skip = 4,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

accel_raw = read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_accel.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(covar_raw)

dim(accel_raw)

accel_raw %>%
  select(SEQN, min1:min5) %>%
  head()
```


```{r clean-covariates}
#clean data
covar_clean = covar_raw %>%
  rename(
    seqn = SEQN,
    bmi = BMI
  ) %>%
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) %>%
  filter(age >= 21) %>%
  mutate(
    seqn = as.character(seqn),
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

glimpse(covar_clean)

covar_clean %>%
  summarise(
    n_participants = n(),
    min_age = min(age),
    max_age = max(age),
    missing_values = sum(is.na(pick(everything())))
  )
```


```{r merge-nhanes}
#Tidy and merge activity data
accel_long = accel_raw %>%
  rename(seqn = SEQN) %>%
  mutate(
    seqn = as.character(seqn)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(minute = as.integer),
    values_to = "mims"
  )

nhanes = covar_clean %>%
  left_join(accel_long, by = "seqn")

glimpse(nhanes)

nhanes %>%
  summarise(
    n_participants = n_distinct(seqn),
    n_rows = n(),
    n_minutes = n_distinct(minute),
    missing_mims = sum(is.na(mims))
  )
```

```{r education-table}
participant_df = nhanes %>%
  distinct(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education)

education_table = participant_df %>%
  count(education, sex) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  arrange(education)

knitr::kable(
  education_table,
  col.names = c("Education level", "Men", "Women"),
  caption = "Number of participants by education level and sex"
)
```


```{r age-distribution, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#age distributions by education and sex
ggplot(
  participant_df,
  aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.12,
    height = 0,
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 1.3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ education,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "blue", "Female" = "pink")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age distributions by education level and sex",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The more-than-high-school group is the largest, with 56 men and 59 women, and generally has younger participants. The high-school-
equivalent group includes more men than women, but women have a higher median age. In the less-than-high-school group, the numbers of men and women are nearly equal, and their age distributions are similar. Ages vary widely within all groups.


```{r total-activity, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#Total activity and age
activity_total = nhanes %>%
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) %>%
  summarise(
    total_activity = sum(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  activity_total,
  aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~education,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "blue", "Female" = "pink")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity(MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Total daily activity generally decreases with age across all education groups, although the trends are not strictly linear. Women tend to have higher activity levels than men in the high-school-equivalent and more-than-high-school groups. Sex differences are less consistent in the less-than-high-school group. Activity levels also vary widely among participants of similar ages.

```{r daily-activity-pattern, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#Activity patterns over 24 hours
activity_by_minute = nhanes %>%
  group_by(education, sex, minute) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_mims = mean(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(hour = (minute - 1) / 60)

ggplot(
  activity_by_minute,
  aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    formula = y ~ x,
    span = 0.15,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~education,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 20)
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "blue", "Female" = "pink")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 6),
    limits = c(0, 24)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Activity patterns over 24 hours",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Mean activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

All three education groups show low activity overnight, a sharp rise in the morning, and a decline in the evening. The less-than-high-school group has a clear peak around noon, with similar daytime patterns for men and women. Women generally have higher daytime activity than men in the other two groups, especially in the more-than-high-school group.

##Problem 3
